find: Atoms are incredibly small — about 0.1 nanometres across.
replace: Atoms are incredibly small — an atom has a radius of about 0.1 nanometres, or \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m.
note: F1: the spec gives the atomic RADIUS as about 0.1 nm; 'across' states it as a diameter, which is out by a factor of two.

find: if an atom was the size of a football, a football would be the size of Earth!
replace: if an atom was the size of a marble, a football would be the size of Earth!
note: F2: the scale analogy was out by about 20x. Scaling an atom (1e-10 m) to a football (0.11 m radius) is a factor of 1.1e9, which would make the football 1.2e8 m - roughly 19 Earth radii. Scaling the atom to a marble (about 6 mm) gives the factor 5.8e7 that turns a football into the Earth.
F3: AQA Combined Science papers are 70 marks in 1 hour 15 minutes; the longest question is a 6-mark extended response. There is no 9-mark item.

expect: Top band (7-9): Detailed evaluation of multiple atomic models, clear explanation of how each advanced understanding, links to broader impact on chemistry. Mid band (4-6): Some evaluation of atomic models with explanations of their contributions. Lower band (1-3): Basic description of one or two models with limited evaluation.
value: Top band (5-6): Detailed evaluation of several atomic models, explaining how each one changed the accepted picture of the atom and why that mattered. Mid band (3-4): Some evaluation of atomic models with reasons for their importance. Lower band (1-2): Basic description of one or two models with little evaluation.
note: F3: band ladder rewritten for 6 marks.
F3: GCSE science carries no SPaG marks and no 12-mark question. 12+4 would be 23% of a 70-mark paper.

expect: Top band (9-12): Comprehensive explanation of formula interpretation, detailed discussion of compound vs element properties, clear scientific reasoning throughout. Mid band (5-8): Good explanation of formula with some discussion of properties. Lower band (1-4): Basic understanding of formula with limited discussion. spelling/grammar marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and specialist terminology (4 marks).
value: Top band (5-6): Clear explanation of what the formula shows about the atoms present, with a well-reasoned comparison of the compound and the elements it is made from. Mid band (3-4): Explains the formula and makes some comparison of properties. Lower band (1-2): Basic reading of the formula with little comparison.
note: F3: band ladder rewritten for 6 marks; SPaG award removed.

expect: Who proposed the plum pudding model of the atom in 1897?
value: Who proposed the plum pudding model of the atom?
note: F4: Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 but set out the plum pudding model in 1904. The spec needs no dates, so the date is removed.

find: Transition metals are found in the central block of the periodic table.
replace: Separate Chemistry only. Transition metals are not examined on Combined Science. They are found in the central block of the periodic table.
note: F5: the Trilogy spec has no transition metals section (5.1.2 stops at Group 7). Labelled rather than deleted.

find: The elements also have lower melting points and higher densities going down the group.
replace: The elements also have lower melting points going down the group.
note: F6: Group 1 density does not rise all the way down - potassium (0.86 g/cm3) is less dense than sodium (0.97 g/cm3). The melting point trend is safe; the density claim is dropped.

find: Concentration can be measured in g/dm³ (mass concentration) or mol/dm³ (molar concentration). Both are essential for different types of calculations.
replace: Concentration can be measured in g/dm³ (mass per volume) or mol/dm³ (moles per volume). Combined Science calculations only need g/dm³; mol/dm³ belongs to separate Chemistry.
note: F7: spec 5.3.2.5 gives concentration only as mass per volume (g/dm3). 'mol/dm' appears nowhere in the Trilogy spec, so calling both units essential is wrong for this qualification.
F8: the question 'One _____ equals 1000 cm3' had two correct options - dm3 (keyed) and litre. The lesson itself states 1 dm3 = 1000 cm3 = 1 litre. Replaced with millilitre, which equals 1 cm3.

find: The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) react vigorously with water and acids. Less reactive metals (zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold) react more slowly or not at all.
replace: Potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium react with cold water. Magnesium, zinc and iron react with dilute acids but only very slowly, or not at all, with cold water. Copper, silver and gold react with neither water nor dilute acid.
note: F9: magnesium reacts with cold water only very slowly and aluminium appears not to react at all because of its oxide layer, so 'react vigorously with water' is a misconception taught as fact. Spec 5.4.1.2 limits these reactions to room temperature and names lithium in the set.

find: The reactivity series (most to least reactive): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au.
replace: The reactivity series (most to least reactive): K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au.
note: F10: spec 5.4.1.2 requires recall of lithium's reactions and places it between sodium and calcium. Lithium was absent from the series students are told to learn.
